Gargi: manager just gave you the Kolkata account as well?
Harish: yep. third new account this quarter 😅
Harish: everyone else "has a lot on"
Gargi: you have three accounts and Nikhil has one
Harish: I know. but she said "you are the only one I trust with this"
Harish: and I hate that it makes me feel taller
Gargi: ok that's honest
Harish: I do feel used. also kind of proud. both at once
Gargi: want me to come with you when you tell her it's too much?
Harish: maybe. let me think first

qa.q: How many accounts does Harish have compared with Nikhil?
qa.a: Harish has three accounts and Nikhil has one.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Harish describe about being trusted with the Kolkata account?
qa.a: Harish feels used and also proud at the same time; being trusted feels flattering even though the workload is unfair.

qa.a: The manager probably thinks Harish will always deliver and may not see the total load; the sentence "the only one I trust" suggests relying on reliability without noticing the cost.

passage: In a small-town post office, Ishita balanced the day's accounts by four, as usual. The postmaster handed her the pension registers as well. "You never make mistakes, Ishita." Deepak, at the next counter, had been on his phone for an hour and was allowed to leave early. Ishita stacked the registers, her jaw tight. She felt used, and yet she stood a little straighter, because the postmaster trusted her. On the way home she rehearsed a sentence to say tomorrow, then dropped it, thinking, they will manage nothing without me.

qa.q: What extra work did the postmaster hand to Ishita?
qa.a: The postmaster handed Ishita the pension registers as well.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Ishita have while stacking the registers?
qa.a: Ishita feels used, with a tight jaw, and also proud, standing a little straighter at being trusted; the two feelings sit side by side.

qa.q: What could Ishita say tomorrow to keep the trust but reduce the load?
qa.a: Ishita could name what she already handles, show the hours involved, and ask the postmaster to share the pension registers with Deepak.

qa.q: How might Deepak see the afternoon, leaving early while Ishita stays?
qa.a: Deepak may not have thought about the extra load on Ishita at all, or may see leaving early as an easy break; nothing in the scene shows Deepak noticing.

grounding: A dependable worker is given extra work because they will always deliver while others coast, feeling used but also proud of being needed.

passage: In the hospital billing office, Divyansh, the supervisor, watched the week unfold. Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday and stayed late on Thursday. Priya at the next desk printed the same three forms and spent long stretches at the tea counter. Nobody had complained. Divyansh noticed Anand's shoulders sagging and Priya's empty in-tray. He weighed it up: if he ignored it, Priya would keep coasting, and Anand would burn out. On Friday he asked Priya for a private word: "I want to understand your workload. Can we look at it together?" Then he took Anand aside and said, "I see how much you have done. Let me rebalance."

qa.q: How many claims did Anand reconcile by Wednesday?
qa.a: Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Divyansh worried about when weighing up what to do?
qa.a: Divyansh was concerned that ignoring the imbalance would reward coasting and burn out Anand; the worry was for fairness and for Anand's health.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do on Friday that a fair manager would do?
qa.a: Divyansh spoke privately with each person, asked Priya about the workload without accusing, and told Anand the effort was seen and would be rebalanced.

qa.q: What might Anand have felt when Divyansh said "I see how much you have done"?
qa.a: Anand probably felt relief and a little pride at being noticed after quietly carrying the load; sagging shoulders suggest that being unseen had been wearing.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and chooses a fair, private conversation over ignoring it.

passage: Dear Francis, I need an outside view. On my team of six, Rahul carries about half the work and Tessa produces about a fifth. I can see it every week in the tracker. Rahul never complains and Tessa always smiles in meetings. I have said nothing for two months, and last week Rahul stayed until nine and looked exhausted. I kept telling myself it would even out. It will not. Next week I will speak privately with each of them, first Tessa, to understand what is going on, then Rahul, to thank him and ask what he needs. Tell me if you think I am being unfair to either. — Zainab

qa.q: How long has Zainab said nothing about the uneven work?
qa.a: Zainab has said nothing for two months.

qa.q: What is Zainab feeling as writing that "it will not" even out?
qa.a: Zainab feels uneasy and a bit guilty for waiting so long, and resolved that ignoring the imbalance is not working.

qa.q: What plan does Zainab make about how to raise the issue?
qa.a: Zainab plans private conversations, first with Tessa to understand what is going on, then with Rahul to thank him and ask what he needs.

qa.q: What might Rahul be feeling after staying until nine while never complaining?
qa.a: Rahul probably feels exhausted and perhaps unnoticed, and may also worry that complaining would look bad; the tiredness shows in staying late.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and plans a fair, private conversation.

passage: Come, have some tea. I will tell you about my second team, the one that never had a fight about work. I am Elizabeth, and back then I led five people. In our very first week we stood at a whiteboard and asked each other: what is fair? Kunal, the youngest, said he could do late testing but not weekends because of his night classes. Someone else said she preferred writing. We agreed on hours, wrote our names next to tasks, and put a tick when each one was done. Every Friday we looked at the board for five minutes. When Kunal's column looked light one week, he said so first, and we moved a task. Nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What did the team do in their very first week?
qa.a: In their very first week they stood at a whiteboard and asked each other what is fair.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when saying first that the column looked light?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt a little nervous but safe enough to be honest, since the team had already agreed openly on what fair looked like and nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What simple habit kept the team from resentment?
qa.a: They wrote names next to tasks, ticked them off, and looked at the board together every Friday for five minutes.

qa.q: What was it like for Kunal to work under the agreed hours because of the night classes?
qa.a: Kunal could do late testing but not weekends, and having that spoken openly meant the limit was accepted rather than hidden as a reason for guilt.

grounding: A team agrees openly what fair effort looks like and tracks it simply, so fairness discussed early avoids resentment later, told by an elder.

passage: Two days before the product launch, Sarika gathered the team of five in the only room with lights, since a power cut had knocked out the rest of the office. "Before we split anything, what does fair effort mean for us?" she asked. Gargi said she could not do nights but could start at six in the morning. Ashok said he wanted a say in who takes the tedious jobs. Nobody dissented; even quiet Ravi murmured, "Let us write it down." On a torn flip-chart page they wrote names, tasks and hours, and drew boxes to tick. By the morning of the launch there were no grudges, only ticks.

qa.q: Why was the team gathered in the only room with lights?
qa.a: A power cut had knocked out the rest of the office.

qa.q: Why does Sarika ask what fair effort means before splitting the work?
qa.a: Sarika wants agreement on fairness before resentment can build; even under time pressure she sees this as protecting the team.

qa.q: What made the agreement easy to follow during the launch rush?
qa.a: They wrote names, tasks and hours on one page and drew tick boxes, so everyone could see who owed what without arguing.

qa.q: What might Ravi be feeling when murmuring "Let us write it down"?
qa.a: Ravi probably feels relieved that a fair and visible plan is forming; being quiet, the written page gives a safe way to have a say.

grounding: A team agrees openly what fair effort looks like and tracks it simply, avoiding slow-burning resentment later, even under time pressure.

passage: In a kindergarten in Seville the teacher tied red bands on half the children and blue on the others for a ball game. Ines, in red, cheered only when the red team threw. When a blue child dropped the ball, Ines laughed and said, "Blue is silly!" Fatima, in blue, glared and shouted, "Red is silly!" A small boy in red, Leo, quietly picked up the blue ball and rolled it back, but nobody noticed. When the teacher swapped the bands at the end, Ines stared at her new blue band and said, very loudly, "I am still red inside."

qa.q: What did Ines say when a blue child dropped the ball?
qa.a: Ines laughed and said, "Blue is silly!"

qa.q: What does Ines's "I am still red inside" suggest about how Ines feels?
qa.a: It suggests that belonging to red has already become part of who Ines is, so being moved feels like losing something, though the bands meant nothing.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next time to soften the sides?
qa.a: The teacher could mix the bands in pairs so red and blue children share a task, giving them a reason to cooperate.

qa.q: What might Leo be thinking when quietly rolling the blue ball back?
qa.a: Leo may simply want the game to keep going, or feels kindly toward the blue child; the small act shows one child not joining the us-and-them.

grounding: Children given different coloured bands quickly favour their own side and dismiss the other, though the groups mean nothing.

passage: At the nursery sports day the teacher gave green caps to one table and yellow caps to the other. For the parade she said, "Everyone hold a partner's hand." Deepak, in a green cap, snatched his hand back from Mahima's yellow cap. "Yellows are slow," he said. Around them three green children nodded and two yellow children scowled. Mahima's lip wobbled. The teacher knelt down and said, "These are only caps. Today we swap." She traded the caps round the group, and Deepak looked at his yellow one, frowning, then held Mahima's hand after all.

qa.q: What did Deepak say about the yellow caps?
qa.a: Deepak said, "Yellows are slow."

qa.q: What might Mahima be feeling when the lip wobbles?
qa.a: Mahima probably feels hurt and rejected, upset at being dismissed for a cap colour that means nothing.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that softened the us-versus-them feeling?
qa.a: The teacher said the caps were only caps and swapped them around, which showed that the colour did not make anyone different.

qa.q: What might it be like for the yellow children who scowled while the green children nodded?
qa.a: The yellow children probably felt angry and defensive, choosing to scowl back at the green side, showing how quickly sides harden.

grounding: Children given different coloured caps favour their own side and dismiss the other, though the groups mean nothing.

passage: My name is Ojas and I am in Blue House. On Sports Day I cheered only when the Blue relay team ran. When Red House won the skipping race, the others in Blue said, "They cheated!" and I shouted it too, even though I had not watched. Nirmala from Red House looked at me and said, "I skipped my best." I felt hot in the face. I said I did not mean her. Later I saw her sitting alone with her medal, and I thought, she is not a Red. She is Nirmala.

qa.q: Which house is Ojas in?
qa.a: Ojas is in Blue House.

qa.q: Why did Ojas shout "They cheated!" without having watched the race?
qa.a: Ojas felt the excitement of belonging to Blue and joined the others' cheering, so the rival side became a little less human; the hot face afterwards shows embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to soften the rivalry after the race?
qa.a: Ojas could go to Nirmala and say well done, since one kind word shows that the other house is made of real people.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when hearing "They cheated!" from the Blue House?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt hurt and proud at once, having done her best; saying "I skipped my best" shows she wanted the true story to be known.

grounding: A child cheers only for their own house and downplays rivals, finding belonging exciting while the other side becomes a little less human.

passage: Note from Shankar Sir after the inter-section quiz. Lakshmi's section, 6B, lost to 6C by two points, and Lakshmi led the booing every time 6C answered. When a 6C child hesitated, six children in 6B whispered, "Wrong! Wrong!" and Lakshmi said, "They always cheat." Nobody in 6B stopped it, though two children looked uneasy. Afterwards I asked the class to name one thing 6C had got right. Lakshmi went quiet, then said, "Their answer about rivers." I plan a mixed-section quiz next week. — Shankar Sir

qa.q: By how many points did 6B lose to 6C?
qa.a: Section 6B lost to 6C by two points.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "They always cheat" about 6C?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt the sting of losing and the pull of belonging to 6B, so blaming the other side felt easier than admitting the loss; the feeling was rivalry mixed with disappointment.

qa.q: What did Shankar Sir do that could soften the rivalry?
qa.a: Shankar Sir asked the class to name something 6C got right and planned a mixed-section quiz, so children work with the other section rather than against it.

qa.q: What might the two uneasy children in 6B have been feeling?
qa.a: They probably felt uncomfortable at the whispering but did not want to break from the group, so they stayed silent.

grounding: A child cheers only for their own section and downplays rivals, with belonging making the other side seem less human.

subtype: Left out for being from elsewhere [Receiver]
passage: Rekha had moved from a big city to the small-town school in the middle of the term. At lunch the girls had already formed their circles: the mango-tree circle, the veranda circle. Rekha stood by the water pot with her tiffin, watching. When she said a word the way she said it back home, two girls giggled, and she stopped speaking. For three days she ate alone. On the fourth day Pranav, a quiet boy, shifted his bag along the bench and said, "There is room." Rekha sat. Nobody said anything, but her shoulders came down for the first time.

qa.q: How many days did Rekha eat alone?
qa.a: Rekha ate alone for three days.

qa.q: How might Rekha have been feeling while standing by the water pot with the tiffin?
qa.a: Rekha felt watchful and a bit invisible, waiting on the edge of formed circles and unsure whether anyone would make room.

qa.q: What small step did Pranav take, and what could a teacher add?
qa.a: Pranav shifted his bag and said "There is room", one kind gesture; a teacher could add a shared task that puts new and old children on the same side.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pranav, a quiet boy, to offer the seat?
qa.a: Pranav may have felt shy and a little brave, as making room in front of the circles is a small risk for a quiet child.

grounding: A new child from another city finds the groups already formed, feels watchful and invisible, and waits for one kind gesture.

subtype: Left out for being from elsewhere [Receiver]
passage: On his first Monday at a school in Gothenburg, Omar stood at the edge of the playground. He knew about ten Swedish words. Groups had formed around the football, the swings and a hopscotch grid, and nobody looked at him. A boy called Elias said something and the others laughed, and Omar could not tell if it was about him. He wandered to the fence and counted bricks. Vera, holding a skipping rope, walked over and held out one end. "Hop?" she said, pointing and smiling. Omar took the end. Nobody spoke, but he turned the rope with care.

qa.q: What did Vera hold out to Omar?
qa.a: Vera held out one end of a skipping rope.

qa.q: What might Omar be feeling while counting bricks at the fence?
qa.a: Omar feels uncertain and left out, unsure whether the laughing was about him; counting bricks gives something to do while waiting for a kind gesture.

qa.q: What made Vera's gesture easy for Omar to accept without shared words?
qa.a: Vera used a rope, a smile and one word, "Hop?", which asks nothing complicated and lets Omar join by doing.

qa.q: How might Elias have seen the new boy at the fence?
qa.a: Elias may not have noticed Omar at all, or may not have known what the laugh meant to someone new; the scene shows nothing of Elias's view.

grounding: A new child from another country finds the groups already formed, feels invisible and watchful, and waits for one kind gesture.

passage: I was sitting on the wall outside tuition when Anjali started imitating the students of the school across the road: "They are all show-offs, they all cheat." Four of us laughed. Dilnaz, beside me, did not, and shifted her bag. Anjali's voice got louder with each laugh and the jokes got sharper. A girl from that school walked by and Anjali went quiet for a moment, then muttered one more joke. I cannot say what Anjali really thinks. Maybe the laughs feel good. But I noticed Dilnaz did not join in.

qa.q: What did Anjali say about the students of the school across the road?
qa.a: Anjali said, "They are all show-offs, they all cheat."

qa.q: Why might Anjali's jokes have gotten sharper with each laugh?
qa.a: Anjali may enjoy the group's approval, which rewards the joke and makes the label spread without being examined; the narrator cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could someone do that keeps friendship but stops the label from spreading?
qa.a: Someone could say "all of them? I know one who is nice", or steer the talk elsewhere, without a lecture, so the joke does not get more laughs.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz be feeling by not laughing and shifting the bag?
qa.a: Dilnaz may feel uncomfortable with the sweeping label but reluctant to speak against the group, which the shifting bag hints at.

grounding: A teenager describes people from another school with sweeping labels, and the group's approval rewards the joke so the label spreads unexamined.

passage: Monday. On the school bus Zubin said the kids from the colony behind the market "never study and always fight." Everyone laughed, and Jatin, next to him, said nothing. Wednesday. Zubin repeated it in the canteen, and a new boy laughed too, eager to be liked. Zubin felt taller. Saturday. At a cricket match Zubin met Rohan from that colony and was stunned: Rohan was polite, an excellent bowler, and ended up lending Zubin a spare pair of gloves. That night Zubin looked at Jatin and, for once, did not make a joke.

qa.q: What did Zubin say about the colony behind the market?
qa.a: Zubin said the kids from the colony behind the market "never study and always fight."

qa.q: Why did Zubin feel taller after the canteen laugh?
qa.a: The group's approval rewarded the joke, so Zubin felt bigger and safer inside the group; the label felt like belonging.

qa.q: What turning point on Saturday changed Zubin's thinking?
qa.a: Meeting Rohan, a polite and excellent bowler who lent spare gloves, showed Zubin a real person that did not match the label.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been thinking when saying nothing on the bus?
qa.a: Jatin may have disliked the sweeping remark but did not want to break from the laughing group, so kept quiet.

grounding: A teenager describes people from another neighbourhood with sweeping labels, the group approves, and meeting an individual shakes the label.

passage: In a school in Hamburg, Freya's turn came to read aloud, and she read with the soft accent of her home language. Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed. Jana laughed too, then looked at her desk. At lunch the group table filled up without a space for Freya. She stood with her tray, heat rushing to her face, and decided that tomorrow she would speak more like them and say less about home. That afternoon the class teacher noticed the empty seat beside Freya, stayed behind after the bell and said, "I heard what happened. It is not your fault, and I will speak to the class tomorrow."

qa.q: What happened when Freya read aloud with the soft accent?
qa.a: Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed.

qa.q: What is Freya feeling when standing with the tray and deciding to speak more like them?
qa.a: Freya feels ashamed and hurt, with anger mixed in, and a wish to hide part of home to be accepted.

qa.q: What turning point that afternoon helped Freya?
qa.a: The class teacher stayed behind, said it was not Freya's fault and promised to speak to the class the next day, which showed that an adult had noticed.

qa.q: What might Jana be feeling after laughing and then looking at the desk?
qa.a: Jana may feel guilty and uneasy, having joined the laughter without meaning harm and now unsure how to make it right.

grounding: A teenager is left out because of their language and accent, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide their identity.

passage: In the college canteen Avni, a scholarship student, put her steel tumbler on the table. "That is from the free-canteen scheme," someone said, and Sudha, the class rep, snorted. Half the table laughed. Avni's face went hot. She thought of telling them she had topped last term's maths, but it sounded like begging. Nobody asked her to the party planning. The next day she copied their way of talking in class and hid her old bag under the seat. On Friday the class mentor, Mr Menon, called her in and said, "I noticed the group leaving you out. That is not okay, and it is not about anything you did. I will raise it with the head today."

qa.q: What did Sudha do when someone mentioned the free-canteen scheme?
qa.a: Sudha, the class rep, snorted.

qa.q: What is Avni feeling when hiding the old bag under the seat and copying the group's way of talking?
qa.a: Avni feels ashamed and wants to blend in, with anger and hurt underneath; hiding the bag shows a wish to hide how different her life looks.

qa.q: What turning point on Friday helped Avni?
qa.a: Mr Menon called Avni in, said the exclusion was not okay and not about anything Avni did, and promised to raise it with the head that same day.

qa.q: How might Sudha, as class rep, see the moment at the canteen table?
qa.a: Sudha may have thought it was only a joke and wanted to fit in with the table, without seeing how it landed on Avni.

grounding: A teenager is left out because of their class background, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide their identity, until an adult acts the same day.

subtype: Meeting the individual behind the label [Response]
passage: "You are from the other school," said Tanuja, folding her arms. "So?" said Sabina, holding one end of a bamboo frame. "We do not like you people." "Which people? I just want the bridge to hold." Their teammate Isha giggled and kept gluing. "Hold the frame straight, Tanuja." They pulled, glued and argued about the angle. "Try it at forty degrees." "Oh, that works!" said Sabina, and grinned, and Tanuja found herself grinning back. By the end of the afternoon Sabina was sharing her lunch, and Tanuja said, "You are not like the stories."

qa.q: What were Tanuja and Sabina building?
qa.a: Tanuja and Sabina were building a bridge from a bamboo frame.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's "You are not like the stories" suggest about how Tanuja's view changed?
qa.a: It suggests Tanuja is surprised and a little embarrassed, having met a real person instead of the label, and now feels warmer.

qa.q: What made the shared work soften the group bias?
qa.a: Building the bridge together gave them a common goal and a problem to solve, so cooperation replaced suspicion.

qa.q: How might Isha have seen Tanuja and Sabina's first exchange?
qa.a: Isha giggled, which suggests amusement at the clash and perhaps relief that the argument stayed light, and then encouraged them to work.

grounding: A teenager gets to know a person from a disliked group through shared work, and cooperation toward a common goal softens the bias.

subtype: Meeting the individual behind the label [Response]
passage: I am Rajni. Before the district tournament our school had to practise with the school we disliked. I had a whole speech ready about them. The coaches paired me with Kunal, their goalkeeper. For twenty minutes we passed the ball. Kunal missed one and laughed: "Sorry, my glove is on the wrong hand." I laughed too. By the water break we were arguing about which team had the worse referee. I still think their supporters are loud, but Kunal is just Kunal now, not one of them. We wanted the same cup.

qa.q: What did Kunal say after missing the pass?
qa.a: Kunal said, "Sorry, my glove is on the wrong hand."

qa.q: How did Rajni's feeling toward the other school change during practice?
qa.a: Rajni went from wanting to give a speech against them to laughing and arguing over the referee, warming to Kunal as a person; the change came through shared play.

qa.q: What made it easy for Rajni to see past the label?
qa.a: The coaches paired Rajni with Kunal to pass the ball, and the shared aim of winning the same cup gave the two a reason to cooperate.

qa.q: How might Kunal have seen Rajni at the start of the drill?
qa.a: Kunal may have felt just as wary, given the rivalry, and the joke about the glove suggests a wish to break the tension.

grounding: A teenager gets to know a person from a disliked group through shared sport, and cooperation toward a common goal softens bias.

passage: I sat behind Tushar in the cafeteria when two boys from our own hostel block spilt trays and shouted at the staff. Tushar shrugged and said, "They just had a bad day." A week later two boys from the other block did the same thing, and Tushar said loudly, "Typical. Those people always behave like this." Ojas, at our table, raised an eyebrow. "You said bad day last week," said Ojas. Tushar blinked. "That was different." I could tell Tushar believed it. I do not think Tushar has noticed the double standard yet.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when two boys from Tushar's own hostel block spilt trays?
qa.a: Tushar said, "They just had a bad day."

qa.q: What does Tushar's "That was different" suggest about what Tushar believes?
qa.a: It suggests Tushar honestly believes the two cases differ and has not noticed the double standard; the blink shows surprise rather than deceit.

qa.q: What could Ojas do next time to help Tushar see it without an argument?
qa.a: Ojas could ask a gentle question, such as "What was different?", and let Tushar answer, instead of only pointing out the contradiction.

qa.q: How might Ojas be feeling when raising an eyebrow and repeating "You said bad day last week"?
qa.a: Ojas is probably a little puzzled or irritated by the unfairness, and speaks up while keeping the tone light enough to leave Tushar room to think.

grounding: A young adult sees a bad act by their own group as an individual mistake but a similar act by another group as typical, a double standard that feels natural.

passage: Monday. After the derby, three fans in Simran's club scarf threw bottles at the away stand. "A few idiots," Simran told Manjula. Wednesday. Photos showed three fans of the other club doing the same. "See? That whole club is savages," said Simran, scrolling. Manjula put down her phone. "Last week it was a few idiots." Saturday. Simran walked past the stand and saw both sets of fans clearing bottles together after a charity match. Simran remembered the words "a few idiots" and said to Manjula, "I said two different things about the same act." Manjula nodded.

qa.q: What did Simran say about the three fans in Simran's club scarf?
qa.a: Simran said they were "a few idiots".

qa.q: What was Simran feeling on Saturday when remembering "a few idiots"?
qa.a: Simran felt a jolt of realisation and some embarrassment at having judged the same act by two different standards.

qa.q: What turning point helped Simran notice the double standard?
qa.a: Manjula quietly repeated "Last week it was a few idiots", and later the sight of both sets of fans clearing bottles together made the contradiction plain.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling when putting down her phone and repeating Simran's earlier words?
qa.a: Manjula was probably uneasy at the unfairness and chose a calm reminder rather than an accusation, leaving Simran room to notice.

grounding: A young adult sees a bad act by their own group as an individual mistake but a similar act by another group as typical, a double standard that goes unnoticed.
